properties.chose:
ONE ATOMIC WRITE PER TOOL CALL, AT THE STORE'S SINGLE WRITE POINT. Everything a call writes (the node body, optional fields, links, edges) commits together or not at all, so a refusal at any later check stores nothing. That fixes all 13 constructors measured, and any future one, and makes "nothing was written" true.

Rejected:
- reordering checks per constructor: it fixes instances and leaves the class open;
- saying in the refusal what was stored: it reports the defect instead of removing it.

Anthony, 2026-10-02: "I accept all your recommendations."
properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. From art:vscode-call-door-field-report-2026-10-02, idea 16 ("Atomic typed writes: validate links and properties before storing anything, or say in the refusal what was stored. Fixes 17"). Triaged 2026-10-02 by triage agent C.

THE QUESTION: 13 typed constructors store the node, then check optional enums, link items or edge types in later writes, so a refusal leaves the node behind. Measured in fact:root-cause-a-typed-constructor-writes-the-node-before-its-later-checks-and-a-refusal-leaves-it-2026-10-02, along with a false "nothing was written" on a revise and a retry that skips the duplicate guard. Which cure?

OPTIONS, none chosen; (a) and (c) are not exclusive.
(a) ONE BATCH PER WRITE CALL, at the call_tool choke point. Every tool marked as a write (read_only_hint false, the predicate the receipt and --call already use) runs inside the store's begin_batch/commit_batch, and an Err discards it. This is the shape of the receipt fix: one place, so a new write joins by being served. The batch already lets reads see its own earlier writes (bulk.rs atomic), which the duplicate guard needs, because it searches with the new node as its baseline. Cheap in code, but it touches every write.
(b) VALIDATE, THEN WRITE, per handler. Build the full property set and resolve every link before the first upsert. This is how add_verification already treats its targets and add_capability its thread, and it lets a refusal list every violation at once (dec:idea-should-a-refusal-teach-every-rule-it-knows-in-one-reply). But it is per handler, which is how the class arose: the next set_optional_props field reopens it.
(c) SAY WHAT WAS STORED: the refusal names what persisted ("the node was written; the link was not"). Honest, and it needs no transaction. But it leaves the half-node, the duplicate-guard bypass and the near-match it then causes.
(d) FIX THE ORDER IN THE 13 HANDLERS: the instance, not the class.

COUNTER-ARGUMENTS, kept:
- A batch at the choke point must also hold back everything a write sets off: the write-generation counter, the auto-export poke, the credit-on-drop touch log, and the preserved-on-write snapshot. Otherwise a discarded call is still credited or exported.
- The fulltext index must honour a discard. There is a test for that (discard_batch_preserves_prior_committed_fulltext), but nobody has tried it on the single-call path.
- Handlers that take the lock twice, or make a network call (external_dependency), need checking.
- (c) alone is cheapest, and is what the reporter's own workaround ("get_node before retrying") already does by hand.
properties.name: ACCEPTED 2026-10-02 — a refused typed write stores nothing: one atomic write per tool call, at the store's single write point
properties.rationale: Recorded open because the cheapest honest answer (c) and the class answer (a) differ in risk, not only in cost, and the choice of where atomicity lives (choke point or handler) is the owner's. The store's batch already exists and is used by import, the bulk forms and draw_edges (dec:bulk-is-all-or-nothing-with-per-item-findings), so (a) asks to extend an existing mechanism rather than to build a new one.
